data.basic-concepts#Basic Concepts:
Prior to modern C++, the values of expression can be roughly categories into lvalue and rvalue by the relative position of value to the assignment operator. Lvalue appears on the left side of assignment while Rvalue is on the right end.
Since C++11, to support the introduction of move semantics, the value categories are refined through two fundamental properties:
Has Identity: Can the object be identified (i.e., located in memory, addressed, persists across statements) Can Be Moved From: Can the object’s resources be transferred to another object Value that has identity is generalized left value (glvalue), while values that can be moved from are right values (rvalue). Glvalue contains lvalue and xvalue (expiring value), Rvalue contains pvalue and xvalue.
Category Has Identity Can Be Moved From Example lvalue ✅ Yes ❌ No x, *p, arr[0] xvalue ✅ Yes ✅ Yes std::move(x), arr[0] prvalue ❌ No ✅ Yes 42, x + y
data.c11-revolution#C++11 Revolution:
C++11 introduced a more refined system with five value categories:
Primary categories: lvalue, xvalue, prvalue Combined categories: glvalue (generalized lvalue), rvalue This change was driven by:
Introduction of move semantics Need for perfect forwarding Rvalue references (Type&&)
data.c17-guaranteed-copy-elision#C++17 Guaran:
C++17 further refined the model by:
Guaranteeing copy elision in certain cases Materializing temporary objects differently Clarifying prvalue materialization
data.evolution-of-value-categories#Evolution:
The evolution of value categories in C++ reflects the language’s growth in handling efficient resource management and perfect forwarding.

data.examples#Examples: // lvalue examples int x = 42; // x is lvalue int& ref = x; // ref is lvalue int arr[10]; // arr is lvalue std::string str; // str is lvalue // prvalue examples int getValue() { return 42; // 42 is prvalue } auto lambda = [](){}; // lambda expression is prvalue 1 + 2; // arithmetic result is prvalue // xvalue examples std::move(x); // result is xvalue std::string().substr() // temporary object from member function static_cast<int&&>(x) // cast to rvalue reference // Understanding combined categories: struct S { int m; }; S().m; // member of prvalue: xvalue std::move(x).m; // member of xvalue: xvalue
data.introduction#Introduction: Value categories in C++ are fundamental concepts that classify expressions based on their properties. Understanding value categories is essential and crucial for modern C++ programming, especially when working with performance optimization through move semantics and perfect forwarding.

Properties over categories Has Identity Can Be Moved From Direct interaction with: Reference qualifiers Template argument deduction Overload resolution
data.pre-c11#Pre-C++11:
In traditional C++ (pre C++11), there were only two value categories:
lvalue: Expressions that refer to a memory location rvalue: Everything else (temporaries, literals) This simple model worked well until the need for move semantics became apparent.

data.pull-latest-commits#Pull latest commits:
From the parent repo, use git submodule update --remote [] to fetch and check out the latest commit on the submodule’s tracked branch (e.g., the one set with set-branch). Omit to update all submodules, or pass a path to update only one. Add --merge to merge into the current branch inside the submodule: git submodule update --remote --merge []. To update all submodules recursively: git submodule update --remote --recursive. If you’ve set the branch with set-branch, you can also cd into the submodule and run git pull as usual.
For the submodule vim tracking main, from the repo root:
# fetch and check out latest commit on main git submodule update --remote vim # or merge into current branch inside vim git submodule update --remote --merge vim
data.track-remote-branch#Track remote branch:
Updating a submodule often leaves it in a detached HEAD. Configure it to track a remote branch instead: git submodule set-branch -b . Use the branch name only (no remote alias, e.g. main not origin/main).
# track remote `main` branch for submodule vim git submodule set-branch -b main vim

data.key-bindings#Key bindings:
Each key binding in tmux belongs to a named key table. There are four default key tables:
root: contains key bindings for keys pressed without the prefix key, prefix: contains key bindings for keys pressed after the prefix key, copy-mode: contains key bindings for keys used in copy mode with emacs-style keys, and copy-mode-vi: contains key bindings for keys used in copy mode with vi-style keys. The default prefix is C-b, and the 2nd prefix is C-a which is GNU screen compatible.
Show key bindings by runningtmux lsk.
